articles.title: The Next Generation Of Law Students Don’t Trust AI Hype
articles.content:
Most revolutions in legal technology rely on the next generation to come in and save the seasoned Luddites from themselves. From desktop computers to the internet, it’s the incoming lawyers who performed the heavy lifting while the senior partners continued printing out emails and sending handwritten replies through interoffice mail.
But as the legal industry dreams of its AI-native future, the next generation of lawyers are a lot less psyched about the technology’s potential. While firms allocate millions (if not a billion) to developing AI tools to take work from the first touch to fully drafted work product, college students don’t trust AI much beyond a fancier research tool.
“The College Student AI Reality Check,” is a new report from Blickstein Group reflecting responses from students across 37 colleges and universities, plus five in-depth interviews. Spearheading the report was Vera Grabow, the group’s intern and a college junior double majoring in History and Political Science, who launched the project based on her own experience watching AI reshape her education and recognizing that no one had actually asked students what they thought about the technology that every press release breathlessly proclaims to be the future of work. “She conceived this project, convinced us to undertake it, wrote the questionnaire, lead the outreach, analyzed the data, and drafted the report,” CEO Brad Blickstein said. “We helped, but this was an exceptional piece of work by a college student.”
The good news for the industry is that students are using AI. Some 71 percent of respondents reported using AI several times a week or more for their schoolwork. Before professors clutch their pearls too tight, the students aren’t turning their assignments over to ChatGPT:
In fact, AI has replaced Google as the preferred first stop for figuring out a new concept, with 27.8 percent reporting that they ping an AI tool first, edging out Google at 25.3 percent. Not that Google isn’t just an AI answer followed by six sponsored links at this point. Both destinations far outpace going to professors and TAs, which clocked in at 3.8 percent. For faculty, office hours remain the best place on campus to be alone with your thoughts.
Research, proofreading, flashcards, brainstorming… those aren’t use cases that excite the greater AI industry. The investors pouring money into the frontier lab furnace expect a technology that will fully replace human labor and allow them to realize their dream of turning poor people into Soylent Green. Meanwhile, the young people most engaged with technology are wary of trusting it as much more than a better search bar and souped up grammar checker.
“I think it’s improved my performance,” a Stanford Earth Systems senior cited in the report said. “I don’t think it has improved my own knowledge.”
Few doubt the technology as a productivity enhancer, but that’s not exactly in line with the “agent drafts the motion while you sleep” pitch that the OpenAI needs if it ever hopes to see enough tokens burned to make ends meet.
The key metric for legal tech is that “acceptable for drafting if substantial edits are made” and less than 8 percent is a brutal number. Employers in every industry will do their best to train its new people to trust the bots, but habits and preconceptions die hard. If most students come out of college skeptical of the tech, it’s going to be hard to either recruit AI enthusiasts or easily rewire disbelievers.
When asked how much time AI actually saves them on a typical assignment, the most common answer is 10-24% of time saved (32.4%), followed by 25-49% (28.2%). Only 8.5% report saving 75% or more, and an identical 8.5% report saving less than 10%. For a tool that many students use on a regular basis, the payoff they describe seems more like an assistant and aid that creates incremental improvements than transformative solutions.
And so much for the technology making itself indispensable in the minds of users:
The report notes that not a single respondent chose “not at all confident.”
A whole 72.1 percent believe heavy reliance on AI leaves people “somewhat” or “much” less capable at their jobs.
Not that students aren’t occasionally doing what they know is probably a bad decision. One respondent had AI digest a two-hour documentary for class rather than watch it. One of the above graphs noted that 46.5 percent use AI to summarize readings. It’s one thing to appreciate a summarizing tool, and another to farm out reading comprehension.
However grim these numbers are for AI, they’re even worse when narrowed to the sample of pre-law students:
These students use AI as often as other respondents, yet are much more skeptical of it: 66.7% say AI is acceptable for brainstorming only, against 38% of the full sample; 66.7% believe heavy reliance will leave them much less capable, against 31.6% overall. Their confidence that they could work without AI is higher (83.3% versus 62%), and their appetite for a collective AI-free semester is 100%, against 80.3% for everyone else.
“A group that uses AI often and trusts it least is not a contradiction,” the report notes, putting these figures in perspective. “Rather, perhaps it mirrors the profession’s instincts showing up early in students who appreciate traits that the law values.” That’s good news for the profession, where AI’s most responsible use case — putting aside true brute force tasks like doc review — is as a teammate overseen by a skeptical human. But it’s not great news for the frontier labs underwriting the supposed revolution.
If AI evangelists want to usher in a new era of work, they’re going to need to spend time persuading this population to trust the technology more. Right now, they’ve got some deeply unsure users who think it’s a fine tutor, but a threat to their own competence. Unless this group learns to get comfortable with a workflow that includes allowing AI to put together a first draft, it’s hard to imagine them entering the workforce capable of getting the most out of these tools even if they wanted to.
My personal experience talking to college students largely tracks this report. A lot of use… a lot of distrust. But I’d been running on vibes. Grabow lives in that world and decided it’s long past time to gather some data.
Check out the full report here.
Joe Patrice is a senior editor at Above the Law and co-host of Thinking Like A Lawyer. Feel free to email any tips, questions, or comments. Follow him on Twitter or Bluesky if you’re interested in law, politics, and a healthy dose of college sports news.

articles.title: The Blue Wave And MTG
articles.content:
Remember Marjorie Taylor Greene, a Republican Congressional representative from Georgia? Elected in 2021, she quit Congress in 2026. She had been an acolyte of 47, having drunk the Kool-Aid. However, on the theory that nothing lasts forever, she became a vocal critic of him during his second term. She favored policies that did not curry his favor, such as expansion of health care coverage, and advocating the release of the Epstein files. 47 then took after MTG. She spit out the Kool-Aid. Was she prescient?
Finally, after years, in fact, decades of elder statespeople clinging to their seats, clueless about the state of their constituents’ worlds, many of them received well deserved boots back to their home states. Instead of retiring with dignity, they suffered ignominious defeats. The Hill called it a “youth quake.” Whatever you choose to call it, it was long overdue.
More than 40 nonincumbent millennials won seats. Gen Z representation tripled. As a dinosaur lawyer (and voter), I am delighted to see that new ways of thinking, creating, and innovating may help how we are governed going forward. While there is certainly value in institutional memory, that memory dims with time’s passage.
A headline in one of the post-slaughter articles of the midterms read (and I am paraphrasing here), that 47 didn’t learn anything. Really? I disagree. 47 did learn something and that is to double down in his final two years in office. He ousted Susie Wiles, his chief of staff, and replaced her with Stephen Miller, a Trump mini-me, and the architect of Trump’s immigration enforcement policies. So those who think the final two years of a lame duck presidency will be better than the first two years are in for a rude surprise. It will be an unpleasant Mr. Toad’s wild ride.
What about all those Biglaw firms that bent a knee or otherwise twisted themselves into pretzels resulting from 47’s second-term flurry of executive orders? Will they now have a change of heart? Will those firms still engage in kissing the ring? Will they unbend those knees that only four of the Biglaw firms never bent? Or will those firms, at least some of them, start to kiss 47 good-bye, and advise him to not let the door hit him on the way out? Lawyers are professional
chameleons, and so it will be fun to see groveling go from red to blue. ATL will have a front-row seat to all of these acrobatics. Break out the popcorn.
So, questions that have no answers, at least not now. What do you think will happen to DEI during the next two years? Will the Mansfield Rule rise from the dead? Do you think that Biglaw and Big Corporate Law will peek out from beyond the curtains that they have been hiding behind over the past two years and resume that which needs to be encouraged, not discouraged? What about a return to, ahem, civility? Will the mud-wrestling language of the past decade, not just by 47 but his minions, diminish over time? Perhaps there will be less bullying and more civility, less nastiness and more courtesy, not just in Washington but across the country. We still have to endure two more years of the Name Caller in Chief.
Jill Switzer has been an active member of the State Bar of California for over 40 years. She remembers practicing law in a kinder, gentler time. She’s had a diverse legal career, including stints as a deputy district attorney, a solo practice, and several senior in-house gigs. She now mediates full-time, which gives her the opportunity to see dinosaurs, millennials, and those in-between interact — it’s not always civil. You can reach her by email at oldladylawyer@gmail.com.

articles.title: The Itty Bitty Sh*tty Committee
articles.content:
Ed. note: This is the latest installment in a series of posts on motherhood in the legal profession, in partnership with our friends at MothersEsquire. Welcome Jeanine M. Donohue back to our pages. Click here if you’d like to donate to MothersEsquire.
Recently, I was invited to dinner with a group of highly accomplished and well-respected women general counsel. I was genuinely excited. It was an opportunity to meet women I admired, hear about their experiences, and learn from them.
Before the dinner, I did what many of us do: I researched the other attendees.
As I read their impressive biographies, I noticed something. I was the only attorney attending who had never served as a general counsel.
I registered that fact and went on with my day.
Or at least I thought I did.
That evening, after spending the day at a professional conference that should have reinforced my confidence and reminded me of my own experience and accomplishments, I got ready for dinner. I intended to walk into that private dining room feeling confident, accomplished, and completely comfortable in my own skin.
Then, somewhere between my hotel and the restaurant, the Itty Bitty Shitty Committee called an emergency meeting in my head. (The concept — and its memorable name — originated with Denise Brousseau, founder of WILpower, an exceptional leadership program for women.)
Most of us know that committee in one form or another.
Mine came prepared with an agenda:
You’ve never been a general counsel.
You’re not a partner at your firm.
Never mind that this has been a conscious and intentional career choice. The committee has never been particularly interested in context.
Then came:
These women are more accomplished than you.
They’re smarter than you.
Why would they be interested in anything you have to say?
By the time I reached the restaurant, I had allowed that internal dialogue to become so loud that I nearly walked past the door. I seriously considered returning to my hotel room and ordering room service.
And then something decidedly less inspirational happened.
It was about 90 degrees outside. I was hot. And I knew the restaurant was air-conditioned.
So I opened the door.
The blast of cold air gave me just enough of a reset to quiet the committee and walk inside.
I am very glad I did.
On the other side of that door was an extraordinary group of women who were accomplished, certainly, but also warm, generous, funny and welcoming.
They engaged with me. They listened to me as I listened to them. We talked about our experiences. We laughed. I learned a tremendous amount.
And at some point during the evening, I stopped thinking about whether I belonged in the room.
I simply belonged in the room.
Looking back, that evening reinforced several lessons I want to remember.
1. A Different Resume Is Not A Lesser Resume.
I had focused on one difference between my career and theirs: they had served as general counsel and I had not.
Without realizing it, I had turned a difference into a deficiency.
But there is no single blueprint for a successful career. We make choices based on our goals, priorities, families, opportunities, interests and sometimes simply where life takes us.
An intentional choice does not become less valid because someone else made a different one.
We should be able to admire another person’s accomplishments without using them to diminish our own.
2. Don’t Reject Yourself Before Anyone Else Has The Chance To Accept You.
This may have been my biggest realization.
Nobody at that dinner told me I didn’t belong.
I did.
Nobody suggested that my experience wasn’t valuable.
I did.
Nobody asked why I had been invited.
I did.
I had been invited into the room, yet I nearly made the decision, on everyone else’s behalf, that I wasn’t qualified to enter it.
That is a particularly insidious form of self-doubt: we can exclude ourselves from opportunities before anyone else has even considered excluding us.
3. Confidence Doesn’t Always Come Before Courage.
We often imagine that successful people feel confident before taking the next step. Perhaps sometimes they do.
But sometimes the order is reversed.
Sometimes you walk through the door while you’re still questioning whether you belong on the other side of it.
Courage does not require the absence of doubt. Sometimes courage is simply refusing to let doubt make the decision.
4. Don’t Compare Someone’s Biography To Your Internal Monologue.
Before the dinner, I knew these women’s titles and professional accomplishments.
What I did not know were their disappointments, difficult decisions, career detours, sacrifices, failures, or moments of uncertainty. I was comparing the polished facts of their professional lives with the unfiltered doubts inside my own head.
Those are never equivalent data sets.
A biography tells you what someone has accomplished. It rarely tells you what they had to overcome, or what they questioned about themselves, along the way.
5. Once You’re Comfortable In The Room, Look For The Person Standing Near The Door.
This may be the most important lesson.
At some point in our careers, each of us becomes comfortable in rooms that once intimidated us.
When that happens, we have an opportunity, and perhaps an obligation, to make the room a little easier for the next person to enter.
Introduce yourself.
Invite someone into the conversation.
Ask a question and genuinely listen to the answer.
Make room at the table.
The women at that dinner had no idea about the internal debate I had been having just minutes earlier. They didn’t know that the Itty Bitty Shitty Committee was still lurking somewhere stage left in my brain.
But through simple acts of warmth, curiosity and inclusion, they silenced it far more effectively than any pep talk I could have given myself.
And that reminded me that we may never know how much a small act of professional generosity matters to someone else.
6. You Were Invited For A Reason.
Perhaps the simplest lesson was the one I almost missed entirely.
I had been invited.
Someone else already believed there was a reason for me to be in that room. My job wasn’t to relitigate the invitation. My job was to show up, participate, listen, contribute and learn.
The Itty Bitty Shitty Committee probably isn’t going anywhere. Mine seems to have appointed itself to a lifetime term.
But I’ve realized that I don’t actually need to eliminate it.
I just don’t have to give it a vote.
So the next time it reminds me that someone else is more accomplished, more credentialed, more important, or more deserving of a seat at the table, I’ll remember that dinner.
Sometimes the most important professional decision we make is simply to open the door and walk into the room.
Although I have also learned that air conditioning helps.
Jeanine M. Donohue is a member of Buchalter’s Litigation Practice Group and Wineries, Vineyards and Breweries Practice Group. She practices in the firm’s St. Helena and San Francisco offices. With over 30 years of experience, Jeanine is a big picture strategist who quickly appreciates the 30,000 foot major issues, while also being attentive to the nuances and important details of each matter she handles. Jeanine maintains a broad litigation practice that includes insurance recovery, commercial, real estate and products liability.

Courage does not require the absence of doubt. Sometimes courage is simply refusing to let doubt make the decision.

4. Don’t Compare Someone’s Biography To Your Internal Monologue.

Before the dinner, I knew these women’s titles and professional accomplishments.

What I did not know were their disappointments, difficult decisions, career detours, sacrifices, failures, or moments of uncertainty. I was comparing the polished facts of their professional lives with the unfiltered doubts inside my own head.

Those are never equivalent data sets.

A biography tells you what someone has accomplished. It rarely tells you what they had to overcome, or what they questioned about themselves, along the way.

5. Once You’re Comfortable In The Room, Look For The Person Standing Near The Door.

This may be the most important lesson.

At some point in our careers, each of us becomes comfortable in rooms that once intimidated us.

When that happens, we have an opportunity, and perhaps an obligation, to make the room a little easier for the next person to enter.

Introduce yourself.

Invite someone into the conversation.

Ask a question and genuinely listen to the answer.

Make room at the table.

The women at that dinner had no idea about the internal debate I had been having just minutes earlier. They didn’t know that the Itty Bitty Shitty Committee was still lurking somewhere stage left in my brain.

But through simple acts of warmth, curiosity and inclusion, they silenced it far more effectively than any pep talk I could have given myself.

And that reminded me that we may never know how much a small act of professional generosity matters to someone else.

6. You Were Invited For A Reason.

Perhaps the simplest lesson was the one I almost missed entirely.

I had been invited.

Someone else already believed there was a reason for me to be in that room. My job wasn’t to relitigate the invitation. My job was to show up, participate, listen, contribute and learn.

The Itty Bitty Shitty Committee probably isn’t going anywhere. Mine seems to have appointed itself to a lifetime term.

But I’ve realized that I don’t actually need to eliminate it.

I just don’t have to give it a vote.

So the next time it reminds me that someone else is more accomplished, more credentialed, more important, or more deserving of a seat at the table, I’ll remember that dinner.

Sometimes the most important professional decision we make is simply to open the door and walk into the room.

Although I have also learned that air conditioning helps.
